title: The special senses
blurb: Follow light through the eye and sound through the ear in the right order, tell rods from cones and hearing from balance.
question: On a night flight, a nursing student notices she sees dim stars better out of the corner of her eye, and as the plane descends her ears feel blocked until they pop. Which photoreceptors explain the first observation, and which ear structure explains the second?

teach.h: Special senses: receptors with their own organs
teach.body: Formally, the special senses are vision, hearing, equilibrium (balance), smell (olfaction) and taste (gustation), each detected by specialized receptor cells housed in organs of the head and carried to the brain by cranial nerves. In plain English: the eye and ear are sense organs that turn light and vibration into nerve signals. For the HESI A2, the high-yield skill is ORDER: the path light takes through the eye and the path sound takes through the ear.

steps.label: Optic nerve
steps.sub: Cranial nerve II to the brain

teach.caption: Light passes the two humors on either side of the lens: aqueous in front, vitreous behind.

head: Structure
Job
rows: Change the shape of the lens

teach.caption: Follow 1 to 5 for the path of light; the optic nerve (6) then carries the signal to the brain. Note that the iris (7) surrounds the pupil and sets how much light gets in.
Night vision and side vision rely on rods; reading and color rely on cones.
Ossicle order from the eardrum inward: malleus (hammer), incus (anvil), stapes (stirrup).
The tympanic membrane separates the outer ear from the middle ear.
Follow 1 to 5 for the path of sound. Note that the semicircular canals (6) sense balance, and the Eustachian tube (7) links the middle ear to the throat.

teach.body: The inner ear does two different jobs. The cochlea, with hair cells in the organ of Corti, converts sound into nerve signals for hearing. The vestibule and semicircular canals sense head position and movement for balance (equilibrium). Both send signals along cranial nerve VIII, the vestibulocochlear nerve. In the middle ear, the auditory (Eustachian) tube connects to the pharynx and equalizes air pressure on both sides of the eardrum.

Smell (olfaction) is the only sense not relayed through the thalamus before reaching the cortex. Taste (gustation) uses taste buds, which detect five basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. Smell travels on cranial nerve I; taste from the front two-thirds of the tongue travels on the facial nerve, VII.

Aaliyah, flying home after her nursing school interview, spots a faint star better when she looks just beside it. That is because rods, which work in dim light and give peripheral vision, are spread across the outer retina, while cones are packed into the fovea where she aims her direct gaze. As the plane descends, her ears feel blocked until she swallows and they pop: her auditory (Eustachian) tubes open and equalize middle-ear pressure with the outside air.

teach.text: Cones give color, not rods. The optic disc is the blind spot; the fovea is the sharpest spot. Ossicles run malleus, incus, stapes from the eardrum. The cochlea is for hearing; the vestibule and semicircular canals are for balance.

items: Light: cornea, aqueous humor, pupil, lens, vitreous humor, retina, optic nerve (II).
The iris sets pupil size; ciliary muscles reshape the lens; the optic disc is the blind spot.
Rods: dim light, black and white, peripheral. Cones: color, sharp detail, fovea centralis.
Sound: auricle, canal, tympanic membrane, malleus, incus, stapes, oval window, cochlea, CN VIII.
Vestibule and semicircular canals = balance; auditory tube equalizes pressure; smell skips the thalamus.

summary: You can now put the structures of the eye and ear in the order light and sound travel through them and explain what each one does. You can also tell rods from cones, the blind spot from the fovea, and the hearing structures from the balance structures.

A.q: Which photoreceptors provide color vision and sharp detail in bright light?
A.why: Cones work in bright light and provide color and sharp detail; they are concentrated in the fovea centralis.

whyNot.0: Rods work in dim light and give black-and-white, peripheral vision.
whyNot.2: Bipolar neurons in the retina pass signals along but are not photoreceptors.
whyNot.3: Ganglion cells carry signals toward the optic nerve; they do not detect color.

A.q: Which structure controls how much light enters the eye by changing the size of the pupil?
A.why: The pupil is the opening in the iris, and the iris adjusts its size.

whyNot.0: The lens focuses light; it does not set the pupil size.
whyNot.1: The cornea is the clear front window that light passes first.
whyNot.3: Ciliary muscles change the shape of the lens for focusing.

A.q: In what order are vibrations passed along the middle-ear ossicles, starting at the eardrum?
A.why: The tympanic membrane vibrates the malleus, then the incus, then the stapes, which pushes on the oval window.

whyNot.1: This is the reverse: the stapes is last, next to the oval window.
whyNot.2: The malleus is attached to the eardrum, so it comes first.
whyNot.3: The incus sits between the malleus and the stapes.

B.q: Which inner-ear structures detect head position and movement to maintain balance?
options: Cochlea and the organ of Corti
Auditory tube and the three ossicles
B.why: The vestibule and semicircular canals of the inner ear sense balance (equilibrium).

whyNot.0: The cochlea and its organ of Corti are for hearing.
whyNot.1: The tympanic membrane and auditory canal collect and transmit sound.
whyNot.2: The auditory tube equalizes pressure and the ossicles transmit sound; neither senses balance.

B.q: Why does the optic disc produce a blind spot in each eye?
options: It contains rods but no cones
It is shaded by the iris
It is where the fovea lies
B.why: The optic disc is where the optic nerve leaves the eye; it has no rods or cones, so light falling there is not detected.

whyNot.1: Rods would still detect light, so a rods-only area would not be blind.
whyNot.2: The iris sits in front of the lens and surrounds the pupil; it does not shade the optic disc.
whyNot.3: The fovea is the area of sharpest vision, the opposite of a blind spot.

B.q: After light passes through the lens, which structure does it travel through next?
B.why: The vitreous humor fills the eyeball behind the lens, and light crosses it to reach the retina.

whyNot.0: Aqueous humor lies in front of the lens, so light passes it earlier.
whyNot.2: The pupil is in front of the lens.
whyNot.3: The cornea is the first structure light passes.

C.q: At dusk, Jamal notices that he sees a faint object more clearly when he looks slightly to one side of it. What best explains this?
options: Cones fill the outer retina and work in dim light
Rods fill the fovea and give sharp detail at night
Rods in the outer retina work best in dim light
Cones in the optic disc are sensitive to dim light
C.why: Rods work in dim light and provide peripheral vision, so looking off to the side places the image on rod-rich retina.

whyNot.0: Cones need bright light and are concentrated in the fovea, not the outer retina.
whyNot.1: The fovea is packed with cones, and rods do not give sharp detail.
whyNot.3: The optic disc has no photoreceptors at all; it is the blind spot.

C.q: During a plane's descent, Tara's ears feel blocked until she yawns and they pop. Which structure has opened to equalize the pressure?
C.why: The auditory (Eustachian) tube links the middle ear to the pharynx and equalizes pressure on both sides of the eardrum.

whyNot.0: The external auditory canal is open to the outside air; it does not connect to the middle ear.
whyNot.1: The semicircular canals sense balance and are in the inner ear.
whyNot.2: The oval window receives vibrations from the stapes; it does not equalize air pressure.

C.q: Which structure receives vibrations directly from the stapes?
C.why: The stapes pushes on the oval window, which passes the vibration into the fluid of the cochlea.

whyNot.1: The tympanic membrane passes vibrations to the malleus, before the stapes.
whyNot.2: The incus passes vibrations to the stapes, not the other way round.
whyNot.3: The auditory tube connects the middle ear to the pharynx; it does not carry vibrations.

reteach.title: The eye as a camera, the ear as a drum
reteach.question: A camera turns light into a picture, and a drum passes a hit along to a microphone. How does each match the eye and the ear?

blocks.body: In a camera, light passes a clear cover, an adjustable opening, a focusing lens and lands on a sensor that sends data down a cable. In the eye: cornea, pupil set by the iris, lens, retina, optic nerve. In the ear, the eardrum is a drum skin. Three tiny levers (malleus, incus, stapes) pass the hit to a small door (oval window) into a fluid-filled shell (cochlea), where hair cells act as the microphone.

blocks.text: The ear's balance sensors (vestibule and semicircular canals) are not part of the drum-to-microphone chain: they sit beside the cochlea and sense motion, not sound.

explain.body: Cornea, aqueous humor, pupil, lens, vitreous humor, retina, optic nerve. The iris sets pupil size and the ciliary muscles reshape the lens.

test.q: Light entering the eye passes through which structure first?
test.why: The cornea is the clear front window of the eye, the first structure light passes through.

whyNot.0: Aqueous humor lies just behind the cornea.
whyNot.1: The pupil comes after the cornea and aqueous humor.
whyNot.3: The lens comes after the pupil.

explain.body: Rods handle dim light, black and white and peripheral vision. Cones handle color and sharp detail and are packed into the fovea centralis. The optic disc has no photoreceptors: the blind spot.

test.q: Which part of the retina gives the sharpest, most detailed vision?
test.why: The fovea centralis is packed with cones, giving the sharpest detail.

whyNot.0: The optic disc has no photoreceptors; it is the blind spot.
whyNot.1: The peripheral retina is rich in rods, which give low detail.
whyNot.2: The choroid is the vascular layer of the eye wall, not part of the retina.

explain.body: Auricle, external auditory canal, tympanic membrane, malleus, incus, stapes, oval window, cochlea (organ of Corti hair cells), then the cochlear branch of cranial nerve VIII.

test.q: Where are the hair cells that convert sound vibrations into nerve signals?
test.why: The organ of Corti in the cochlea holds the hair cells for hearing.

whyNot.0: The semicircular canals sense head movement for balance, not sound.
whyNot.2: The tympanic membrane vibrates but does not convert sound into nerve signals.
whyNot.3: The auditory tube equalizes middle-ear pressure.

explain.body: The vestibule and semicircular canals sense balance. The auditory tube links the middle ear to the pharynx. Smell is the only sense not relayed through the thalamus first; taste buds detect sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami.

test.q: Which sense reaches the cerebral cortex without first being relayed through the thalamus?
test.why: Smell (olfaction) is the only sense not relayed through the thalamus first.

whyNot.0: Taste signals are relayed through the thalamus.
whyNot.1: Hearing signals pass through the thalamus on the way to the auditory cortex.
whyNot.2: Visual signals are relayed through the thalamus to the occipital lobe.
